definition: A shrink-resist treatment that degrades or coats the cuticle scales of wool so that the fiber can be machine washed with little felting shrinkage.
explanation: Wool felts because its cuticle scales create a directional friction effect: fibers slide more easily one way than the other, so agitation in warm, wet conditions ratchets them into a denser mat. Superwash processes reduce that effect in two ways. An oxidative step, classically acid chlorination, degrades the outer cuticle surface and makes it more hydrophilic; a polymer step then deposits a thin resin film that masks the scale edges. The combined chlorine-resin route is the traditional industrial method and can be applied to tops, yarn or garments.
example: A sock yarn is sold in two versions from the same Merino top, one untreated and one superwash. A student washes a swatch of each in a warm machine cycle and measures area shrinkage. The untreated swatch shrinks and firms visibly, while the treated one stays close to size. The exercise shows that the finish, not the fiber diameter, is doing the work.
caution: Superwash describes a finish, not a breed or grade, and it changes more than washability: treated wool usually feels smoother, dyes differently and cannot be deliberately felted or fulled. The chlorine route generates environmentally harmful organic halogen byproducts, and chlorine-free alternatives carry their own trade-offs. A machine-washable label depends on a tested care regime, not simply on the word superwash.
deeper: In the chlorine-resin route, wool is chlorinated under acidic conditions, which oxidizes the disulfide-rich surface proteins and strips part of the fatty outer layer; a cationic polyamide-epichlorohydrin resin is then applied and cured as a film that masks scale edges and narrows the friction difference between sliding with and against the scales. Because of its halogenated byproducts, research targets alternatives. Proteases alone act poorly on the hydrophobic outermost cuticle and can attack the cell membrane complex inside the fiber, costing strength. Pairing them with disulfide-reducing agents such as sodium thioglycolate, sodium sulfite or TCEP has given laboratory felting shrinkage of about 4 to 6% with limited strength loss. Performance is judged by area shrinkage after a specified number of machine-wash cycles.
origins: Shrink-resist research intensified as domestic washing machines spread in the mid-twentieth century. The chlorine-resin method called Chlorine-Hercosett, named for the Hercosett resin used in its polymer step, became the traditional industrial process. Superwash became the trade shorthand for wool treated to survive machine washing, and recent work on enzymes combined with reducing agents aims to replace the chlorine step without sacrificing fiber strength.

definition: The breaking force of a fiber or yarn divided by its linear density, a mass-normalized strength usually expressed in centinewtons per tex or grams-force per denier.
explanation: Because fibers and yarns are too fine and irregular to measure cross-sectional area easily, textile strength is normalized by linear density, mass per length, instead of by area. A single fiber or yarn is clamped and extended at a controlled rate until it breaks; the peak force divided by its tex or denier gives tenacity. This lets fibers of very different fineness be compared on one scale. Tenacity is measured on conditioned samples, and many fibers are also tested wet, since water weakens some fibers markedly and affects others little.
example: Two yarns break at the same force, but one weighs twice as much per kilometer. Dividing each breaking force by its tex shows the lighter yarn has twice the tenacity, meaning its material is stronger for its mass. A designer choosing a lightweight but durable sailcloth yarn would compare tenacity rather than raw breaking force.
caution: Tenacity is not the same as tensile stress in pascals, which divides force by area; converting between them requires fiber density. It also differs from breaking force, which depends on how much material is present. Tenacity depends on test conditions such as gauge length, extension rate, humidity and whether the sample is wet, so values from different methods are not directly comparable.
deeper: Arithmetic links the units: 1 gram-force is 9.807 mN and 1 denier is 1/9 tex, so 1 gf/den = 9.807 x 9 mN/tex, about 88.3 mN/tex or 8.83 cN/tex, and 1 gf/tex is about 0.98 cN/tex. Stress in megapascals equals tenacity in N/tex times density in g/cm3 times 1,000, so 1 cN/tex corresponds to 10 x density MPa; for PET (about 1.38 g/cm3), 50 cN/tex is roughly 690 MPa. Tenacity rises with the molecular orientation produced by drawing and falls when fillers are compounded into the polymer. Published values show the spread: one comparison reported lyocell at about 32 cN/tex dry and 29 wet, viscose loses close to half its tenacity when wet, and an enzyme-treated sisal fiber reached about 38 cN/tex.
origins: Textile strength has long been normalized by linear density because fine, irregular fibers make cross-sectional area hard to measure. Grams per denier followed from the denier count used for silk and filament yarns. The tex system, described by A. G. Scroggie in Textile Research Journal in 1958 and later published by ISO as ISO 1144, gave a metric base, and centinewtons per tex became the usual SI expression, although grams per denier remains common in filament trades.
